Blurred describes something that is not clear, not sharp, or not well-defined — something whose edges, details, or divisions are difficult to make out.

The best way to grasp it is through contrast. Think of a clear photograph versus a blurred one. In a clear photo, every detail is sharp — you can see the exact outline of every object, fine textures, precise edges. In a blurred photo, everything looks smudgy or fuzzy. Outlines become soft, details disappear, and things that should be separate seem to melt into one another. That experience — of something losing its sharpness and becoming hard to distinguish — is the heart of what "blurred" means.

In its most literal use, blurred describes things that the eye cannot see clearly. Blurred vision means your eyes can't focus properly, so everything around you appears fuzzy and indistinct — the way things look when you first wake up, or when someone who needs glasses looks at a sign. A blurred photograph is one that came out of focus, perhaps because the camera shook or the subject was moving too fast. A blurred figure in the distance is one you can't quite make out — you can see something is there, but not clearly enough to identify it.

The defining quality in the visual sense is that edges and details are not sharp. Things that should appear distinct look like they're softening and bleeding into each other.
In the abstract sense — blurred lines and boundaries

This is where "blurred" becomes especially powerful and widely used. It describes situations in life, thought, or society where two things that are supposed to be clearly separate have become mixed, overlapping, and hard to tell apart.

Imagine two countries with a sharp, clear border between them. Now imagine that in real life, people on both sides speak the same language, follow the same customs, and nobody quite agrees where one country ends and the other begins. That real-world line has become blurred.

This kind of usage appears everywhere in English. "Working from home has blurred the boundaries between professional and personal life" — because when your office is your living room, the clear separation between work time and personal time dissolves into something messy and undefined. "The line between fact and fiction has become blurred in modern media" — because it's increasingly hard to tell real news from invented stories. "The blurred distinction between art and advertising" — because some commercials are made with so much creativity and beauty that they feel indistinguishable from art.

In every case, the pattern is the same: two things that were clearly separate have lost the sharp division between them, and it has become difficult — sometimes impossible — to tell where one ends and the other begins.
In the context of memory and perception

"Blurred" also describes memories and mental experiences that are vague and imprecise. "My memories of that summer are blurred" means you can't recall the details with clarity — you know things happened, but the specifics are hazy and uncertain, much like a photograph that didn't come out sharp. "A blurred sense of reality" describes a state of mind where a person's grasp of what is real and what isn't lacks precision — things feel indistinct and uncertain in the mind.

No matter how it's used, blurred always conveys a sense of lost definition. Something that was — or should be — clearly defined has lost that quality. It has become fuzzy, hazy, or indistinct. And this almost always makes things harder to work with: a blurred photo is harder to interpret, a blurred boundary is harder to respect or enforce, a blurred memory is harder to rely on and trust.

So when you see the word "blurred," ask yourself: what was the clear, sharp thing that has now lost its clarity? That will always point you to the exact meaning in context.
The most common phrases you'll encounter

Blurred lines is perhaps the most common — it means the separating line between two things is no longer clear. Blurred boundaries refers to roles, spaces, or categories that are not well-defined. Blurred vision is the everyday and medical term for eyesight that is fuzzy and out of focus. Blurred memories are recollections that are hazy and imprecise. A blurred image is simply a picture that is out of focus.

Something is blurred when it lacks sharpness, clarity, or clear definition — whether you are looking at it with your eyes, or trying to determine where one idea, category, role, or concept ends and another begins.
